Once a stimulus set exists, it has to be presented in an experiment. `lexsync`
generates that experiment from a declarative description of the trial. A trial is a
list of events. Each event says what appears, for how long and whether a hardware
trigger is sent at its onset, and each presentation target interprets that same
list. One engine therefore serves several paradigms and three targets, and adding a
paradigm means writing a new event list without changing the backends.

This vignette covers the event model, the paradigm registry, the three targets
and how they differ, the trigger timing that motivates the design, and how to add
a paradigm. It runs on the bundled English example lexicon and writes everything
to a temporary directory.

```{r setup}
library(lexsync)
schema <- yaml::read_yaml(
  system.file("extdata", "schema.yaml", package = "lexsync")
)
lex <- load_lexicon(
  system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  schema, language = "english"
)
pool <- build_pool(lex, list(length = c(3, 7), frequency = c(3.8, 7.0)))

design <- list(
  name = "vignette_experiment", language = "english", n_per_condition = 12,
  paradigm = "factorial",
  conditions = list(
    list(name = "high", define_by = list(frequency = c(5.2, 7.0))),
    list(name = "low",  define_by = list(frequency = c(3.8, 4.4)))
  ),
  match_on = list("length", "n_density", "old20"),
  counterbalance = list(lists = 1)
)
stim <- match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)
stim <- counterbalance(stim, design, schema)
head(stim[, c("trial", "list", "set", "condition", "word")], 3)
```

## The trial-event model

A design's trial is a list of events. Each event is a plain list whose `type`
selects the behaviour and whose remaining fields parameterise it. The factorial
paradigm's default sequence is a fixation cross, the word, a response window and
a blank.

```{r events}
events <- resolve_events(design)
str(events)
```

`resolve_events()` is the accessor the backends use. It returns a design's own
`events` list if it has one, and otherwise the default sequence of the design's
paradigm. The eight event types are `fixation`, `text`, `mask`, `blank`,
`region_by_region`, `response`, `question` and `feedback`. `fixation`, `text` and
`mask` draw something for the event's duration, and `blank` draws nothing for it.
`response` and `question` collect a keypress. `region_by_region` presents a
segmented sentence one region at a time, advancing on a key. `feedback` scores the
keypress just collected and reports it, and is described under 'Practice, fillers
and feedback' below.

Durations are given in milliseconds, as `duration_ms`. That is the unit a
methods section reports and the unit all three targets present, so a design asks
for the same interval wherever it runs. How closely each target delivers it
differs, as described below. A visual stimulus can still only appear on a
refresh, so the PsychoPy script measures the display's refresh rate when it starts
and converts each duration into the nearest whole number of flips: 50 ms is three
flips at 60 Hz and seven at 144 Hz. The trigger stays bound to the flip.

The other two targets time their events differently. The generated OpenSesame
experiment builds every canvas of a trial before the trial starts and times each
event from the onset its display returns. It ends the event half a frame before its
duration is up, so that the next display appears on the refresh that ends it. On a
simulated display at 60, 120 and 144 Hz, the prime and the mask of the `priming`
paradigm then last the flips the PsychoPy script gives them. The paradigm's 83 ms
stimulus-onset asynchrony stays 83.3 ms at all three rates. A duration within a
millisecond or so of halfway between two whole numbers of flips can still come out
a flip longer or shorter than in PsychoPy. In the browser, timing varies with
the machine and the browser, and primes of 33 to 50 ms are not reliably realised
online. Whatever the target, verify the timing a study depends on with a photodiode,
as described under 'Checking the timing' below.

A duration may also be given as `duration_frames`, as several registered paradigms
give theirs, and an event that gives both uses `duration_ms`. A frame count is
converted to milliseconds when the design loads, at
`presentation.assumed_refresh_hz` in the schema, 60 by default. The count therefore
refers to frames at that assumed rate and not at the rate the experiment runs at.
The `timeout_ms` of a response window is always in milliseconds, because a response
deadline is not tied to the refresh.

A text event's `case`, `upper` or `lower`, sets the letter case its text is shown
in. The runners apply it as they show the text, with `str.upper()` and
`str.lower()` in PsychoPy and OpenSesame and `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` in
jsPsych, so the loop tables and the data files keep each item as it was written.
lexsync never changes the case itself, because `toupper()` leaves the German sharp
s as it is where Python and JavaScript give 'SS', and the two engines must write the
same files.

A mask's `length_of` names fields of the trials, and its one-character content is
repeated as many times as the longest of their values has characters, counted when
the experiments are written:

```yaml
- type: mask
  content: '#'
  length_of: [prime, target]
  duration_ms: 500
```

The count is in characters, not bytes, over every trial of every list, so each
target and each list shows the same mask.

### When a response is collected

A response event after a text event collects its key from that stimulus's onset.
The stimulus stays on screen for its duration at most and a blank follows it. The
window closes once the stimulus's duration and the response's `timeout_ms` have
both passed, so the factorial design here collects for 2,800 ms from the word's
onset. A key pressed while the word is still visible counts, the first key ends the
trial, and every target times the reaction from the word's onset.

A design that asks the participant to wait, as a delayed-response EEG design does,
keeps a window that opens once the stimulus has gone:

```yaml
- type: response
  keys: [f, j]
  timeout_ms: 2000
  from: offset
```

A stimulus that should stay on screen for the whole window, as the
`masked_priming` target does, takes the window's length as its duration, and its
response a `timeout_ms` of 0.

By default, a response after any other event is collected from the offset, so one
that follows a blank keeps the window it had, timed from the window's own onset.
`from: onset` after such an event is rejected, since a window from the onset opens
with a text event and none comes right before it. The datasheet records each
response window as `presentation$response_windows`, and its Methods text says when
responses were collected.

### Instructions and the response mapping

Every generated experiment shows instructions and waits for the space bar before
its first trial. The participant reads them at their own pace, and the
experimenter can start the run when the participant is ready. A design gives its
own text under `instructions`, which may hold line breaks:

```yaml
instructions: |
  You will see a string of letters.
  Press F if it is a real English word and J if it is not.
```

The text is carried as data: JSON in the PsychoPy script and the jsPsych page, and
an escaped literal in the OpenSesame script, so nothing in it can become code. A
control character other than the line break is rejected.

When a design gives no `instructions`, lexsync writes English instructions that
depend on the task. For a lexical decision, they name the keys for a word and a
pseudoword. For a categorisation, they say that the first key means yes and the
second no, and they say the same of a comprehension question's keys. In any other
design, the factorial one here among them, they say only which keys to press, and
the run log asks for instructions that say what each key means. The run log also
notes a design in another language that gives no text of its own. The targets' own
short messages, such as the prompt to press the space bar, are in English.

A lexical decision maps word to its response event's first key and pseudoword to
its second. The paradigm's events therefore map word to the left arrow key, and
`design_en_lexdec_blocks.yaml`, whose events use f and j, maps word to f, as its
practice table does. A design may give its own mapping, with keys its response
event allows, and may rotate it across lists:

```yaml
response_mapping: {word: j, pseudoword: f}
rotate_mapping_by_list: true
```

When the mapping is rotated, each key in list *k* moves *k* - 1 places along the
response event's keys, and each version's instructions name its own keys. With two
keys, the rotation swaps them in every even-numbered list. A mapping is rejected if
it names a key the response event does not allow, if it gives no key for a
condition whose trials name no answer, or if it names a condition no trial has.

`export_experiments()` gives each trial its correct key in `answer` as it assigns
the trigger codes, so every trial of a lexical decision can be scored. The stimuli
file does not change. A practice or filler table keeps its own answers, and the run
log notes any that the mapping contradicts, as a rotated mapping does in its
even-numbered lists. jsPsych records a key by the browser's name for it, so the
jsPsych page names each answer that way, `arrowleft` for `left`, and in every
target a correct response equals its trial's answer. The datasheet records the
mapping as `presentation$response_mapping`, and its Methods text says which key the
participants pressed for which condition.

### Content and field references

An event's `content` is either a literal or a reference to a column of the trial
table. A reference is a single field name in braces, and it makes the event list
a template that serves every trial in the design.

```{r content}
lapply(events[1:2], function(ev) ev$content)
```

The fixation event's content is the literal `+`, which every trial shows.
The text event's content is `{word}`, so each trial shows its own row's `word`
column. `required_fields()` resolves the references into the columns a design's
items must carry, and a design's item table is validated against them before
anything is generated.

```{r required-fields}
required_fields(design)
required_fields(list(paradigm = "priming"))
required_fields(list(paradigm = "self_paced_reading"))
```

Presented strings are always carried as data. Each target writes a trial table and
reads the strings from it at run time, and they are never interpolated into generated
code. An apostrophe in a stimulus therefore cannot break a generated script.
`load_items()` also rejects control characters and over-long values in the fields
a paradigm presents.

### Triggers on an event

An event may carry a `trigger`. Three forms are accepted, and the form sets what
the EEG marker means.

```{r triggers-in-events}
priming_events <- PARADIGMS$priming$events
or_dash <- function(x) if (is.null(x)) "-" else as.character(x)
data.frame(
  type = vapply(priming_events, function(e) e$type, character(1)),
  content = vapply(
    priming_events, function(e) or_dash(e$content), character(1)
  ),
  trigger = vapply(priming_events, function(e) or_dash(e$trigger), character(1))
)
```

The literal integer 20 on the prime marks every prime with the same code, since
what is being timestamped is the prime's appearance. The token `"condition"` on
the target resolves per trial to that trial's condition code, which is the marker
an ERP analysis will epoch on. The token `"item"` resolves to a per-item code.
Events with no trigger send nothing.

A literal code must be a whole number from 1 to 255, the values one byte on the
port can carry. Anything else, a misspelt token such as `"conditon"` included, is
rejected when the experiment is generated, with a message naming the event. A
literal of 254 or 255, which the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments send when the
session starts and ends, is reported then. One equal to a condition code the design
sends is reported too, as is one within the range of the item codes it sends.

The tokens are resolved by `assign_triggers()`, which computes the codes and adds
them as columns.

```{r assign-triggers}
trig <- assign_triggers(stim)
unique(trig[, c("condition", "condition_trigger")])
range(trig$item_trigger)
```

Condition codes start at 101 and count up in order of first appearance, unless
`assign_triggers()` is given the order through its `conditions` argument. The
order of first appearance in a shuffled trial list depends on the seed, so an
analysis that decodes the codes should not rely on it. `export_experiments()`
therefore passes the order of the design's `conditions` entries. The pipeline does
the same and adds any other condition in the order the item source lists it, such
as the words before the pseudowords of a generated lexical decision. Under every
seed, the first condition the design lists is 101.

```{r assign-triggers-order}
unique(assign_triggers(stim, conditions = c("high", "low"))[
  , c("condition", "condition_trigger")])
```

Item codes run from 40 upwards in code-point order of the set labels, and once a
design has ten sets or more, that order is not the numeric one. With sets 1 to 20,
set 10 takes 41 and set 2 takes 51. Decode an item code through the loop table,
which pairs each trial's set with its code, and never from the label.

```{r item-codes}
twenty <- assign_triggers(data.frame(condition = "a", set = 1:20))
stats::setNames(twenty$item_trigger, twenty$set)
```

Item codes stay below 240, since a code is one byte and 254 and 255 mark the
session. A design may send item codes together with condition codes, or with a code
of its own from 40 to 239. Its item codes are then drawn from the codes those leave
free, skipping 101 upwards and the design's own codes. Otherwise, sets 65 and 66 of
a 70-set design would take 101 and 102, and an analysis that cuts its epochs at the
condition codes would also catch two items. Such a design is rejected when it has
more item sets than free codes, unless the schema sets
`triggers.allow_code_overlap: true`, which lets the item codes wrap and repeat
within the free codes. Any other design takes its item codes from 40 upwards, in
code-point order of the set labels. They wrap at 200 values, so a design with more
than 200 item sets reuses item codes.


### Timing that varies from trial to trial

A duration need not be the same on every trial. An event may instead declare a
`duration:` block, in one of two forms:

```yaml
- type: text
  content: '{prime}'
  duration: {from_column: prime_ms}          # read per trial from the items
- type: blank
  duration: {jitter: [400, 800], as: iti_ms} # drawn per trial, in milliseconds
```

The two exist for different reasons. A duration read from a column is a
manipulated variable. Here it is the prime's duration, which with the mask that
follows sets the stimulus-onset asynchrony, the variable manipulated to separate
automatic from strategic processing. It belongs in the item table and in the
analysis. A jittered duration is not manipulated and decorrelates the design
matrix, as EEG and fMRI designs routinely require.

Neither draws a random number. A jittered value is a uniform integer keyed on the
seed, the column name, the list, the set and the condition, so both engines
realise the same milliseconds and a rerun reproduces them. Because the column name
is part of the key, two jittered events draw independently.

Either form writes the realised milliseconds into the stimuli table and the loop
table, since the analysis needs them. `config/design_en_priming_jitter.yaml` is a
worked example carrying both. Its prime lasts `prime_ms` and a 33 ms mask follows,
so its stimulus-onset asynchrony is `prime_ms` plus 33 ms.

Every value read from a column must be a finite, non-negative number of
milliseconds. A blank or negative cell is rejected with a message naming the column
and the trial's set and condition. Left alone, it would give an experiment that
stops at the blank or shows the stimulus for no time at all. Fractional
milliseconds, such as the 33.333333 that an item table built on 60 Hz frames
carries, are rounded once with the rounder both engines share and written back. The
stimuli, the loop tables and all three targets then present the same whole
milliseconds, and the run log counts the values rounded. A fixed `duration_ms` or
`duration_frames` is checked the same way, and the lower bound of a jitter must not
be negative.

## The paradigm registry

A paradigm bundles a default event sequence with the fields it needs and the
recipe for counterbalancing it. `PARADIGMS` is the registry, and it is exported,
so it can be read to see what a design will inherit.

```{r registry}
names(PARADIGMS)
data.frame(
  paradigm = names(PARADIGMS),
  fields = vapply(
    PARADIGMS,
    function(p) paste(p$stimulus_fields, collapse = ", "),
    character(1)
  ),
  counterbalance = vapply(
    PARADIGMS, function(p) p$counterbalance, character(1)
  ),
  n_events = vapply(PARADIGMS, function(p) length(p$events), integer(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

`factorial` shows a matched word per trial. `lexical_decision` is the same shape
but presents a `target`, which is a real word or a generated pseudoword.
`priming` is backward pattern-masked: a 50 ms prime and a 33 ms `#####` mask come
before the target, so the stimulus-onset asynchrony is 83 ms at 60 Hz. There is no
forward mask, and prime and target keep the item table's letter case.
`masked_priming` has the arrangement of Forster and Davis (1984): a forward mask of
hash marks, a brief prime in lower case and the target in upper case.
`self_paced_reading` replaces the word event with a region-by-region sentence and
adds a comprehension question. `categorisation` shows a category cue and then the
word to judge against it.

In `masked_priming`, the mask has as many marks as the longest prime or target has
characters. By default, lexsync shows it for 500 ms, the prime for three frames
(50 ms at 60 Hz) and the target until the response or for 2,000 ms. Without the
forward mask, a prime of 50 ms is usually visible. The change of case keeps a
related prime and its target from sharing their visual form, so that priming does
not arise from the overlap of the two displays.

`design_en_rastle_repro.yaml` uses `masked_priming` for the Rastle, Davis and New
(2004) reproduction. It is a lexical decision whose nonword targets are fillers
with the right arrow key as their answer, and its response mapping puts both
priming conditions on the left. `design_en_andrews_repro.yaml` runs the Andrews
(1989) reproduction as a lexical decision the same way, with one pseudoword per
selected word. Both designs' comments say how the fillers were made and what still
differs from the original studies.

What separates `categorisation` from lexical decision is where the question is
asked. The category cue is a trial event, shown afresh each time, since the
category varies from trial to trial. Crossing one word with two cues is how a
categorisation study separates a property of the word from the demands of the
task. A robin is a bird quickly and an animal slowly, and only the question
changed.

The `answer` field of a categorisation holds the key that is correct on the trial,
so scoring is a string comparison against the recorded response. Because the
paradigm requires the field, the PsychoPy and OpenSesame targets can score each
response against it, and the jsPsych data rows carry it beside the response. A
categorisation also needs 'no' trials, or pressing the yes key on every trial
scores perfectly. In `design_en_categorisation.yaml`, 16 foils, nouns that do not
belong to the category they appear under, are fillers with the answer j.

Each paradigm's `counterbalance` entry names one of two recipes. The factorial
recipe shows every matched item and splits the matched sets across lists. Under it,
a design with more lists than item sets is rejected, since the surplus lists would
be empty. The Latin-square recipe exists because, in `priming`, `masked_priming`,
`self_paced_reading` and `categorisation`, the same target appears in more than one
condition. Showing a participant both the related and the unrelated version of one
target would let them see the manipulation, and showing the same word under both
category cues would turn the second presentation into a repetition-priming trial.
The Latin square gives each item exactly one condition per list and rotates it
across lists, so no target repeats within a list.

```{r counterbalance-recipes}
table(list = stim$list, condition = stim$condition)
```

The paradigm decides the recipe whether or not a design lists its own events, so a
priming design that reads its prime's duration from the items keeps its Latin
square. `counterbalance.recipe` names a recipe outright, `factorial` or
`latin_square_target`, for a design that needs the other one.

A Latin-square rotation is complete only when the lists and the item sets are
multiples of the number of conditions. One list confounds item and condition, since
every participant sees each item in the same condition. Two lists for three
conditions show each item in only two of them, and nine items in two conditions
leave each list with five trials in one condition and four in the other. The run
log and the datasheet report such a rotation, and the Methods text calls it
incomplete. With `counterbalance.incomplete: error` in the design, or in the schema
for every design, such a rotation is rejected. The datasheet's
`counterbalancing` record gives the recipe that ran, the lists the stimuli table
holds, whether the rotation is complete and the trials each list gives each
condition.

### Trial orders and runs of one condition

One seed gives each list one order, and every participant given that list sees
it, so each item sits at the same serial position for all of them. The order also
has runs of one condition as long as a uniform shuffle gives. Over seeds 1 to 1000
of a lexical decision with 60 words and 60 pseudowords, the longest run had a
median of 7 and a maximum of 21. A run of seven is seven trials in a row with the
same correct key. Two settings change this, and both are off by default.

```yaml
counterbalance:
  lists: 2
  max_run: 2
  orders: 3
```

`max_run: k` caps every run of one condition at k trials, or of one value of the
column `run_on` names, where a missing value counts as a value of its own. This is
the kind of sequence constraint that pseudorandomisation programs such as Mix
impose (van Casteren & Davis, 2006). The cap is applied by a repair of the seeded
order that keeps as much of that order as the limit allows. Each step takes the
earliest remaining trial in the seeded order that neither extends the current run
beyond k nor leaves the rest of the list unable to keep the limit. Without this
look-ahead, the repair ran out of trials near the end of 931 of 1,000 seeded orders
of a list of 40 words and 80 pseudowords at k = 2, a limit that some order of that
list keeps. With it, only a limit that no order can meet is rejected, and the
message gives the counts that rule it out, such as 80 pseudoword trials against 40
others at k = 1. With fillers, the limit applies to the order they are interleaved
in, and the practice trials keep it on their own.

`orders: m` writes m orders of each list into the loop tables, as `order_1` to
`order_m`, each trial's position in each order. Order 1 is the seeded order, and
orders 2 to m are ranked by the same keyed hash with the order's number in the key,
each repaired under `max_run`. The experiments choose an order by participant
number. Participant *p* runs version `((p - 1) mod V) + 1` in order
`(((p - 1) div V) mod m) + 1`. The participants given one version therefore run
its orders in turn, and a run without a participant number runs order 1.
OpenSesame, whose loop presents its table in file order, gets one experiment per
version and order. The orders are stored in the loop tables, which both engines
write byte for byte, so the browser page needs no hashing of its own. The
datasheet's `counterbalancing` record gives the limit, the longest run realised in
each version and the number of orders, and the Methods text states them.

```{r trial-orders}
limited <- utils::modifyList(design, list(counterbalance = list(lists = 1, max_run = 2,
                                                                 orders = 2)))
ordered <- counterbalance(stim, limited, schema)
head(ordered[order(ordered$order_2), c("trial", "order_1", "order_2", "condition", "word")])
```

### Balanced list assignment

The factorial deal sends set 1 to list 1, set 2 to list 2 and so on. That is
reproducible, but it balances nothing. Every *n*th set goes to the same list, so a
dimension that happens to vary smoothly across sets is dealt out unevenly. Where
each list goes to a different group of participants, the unevenness is confounded
with the group.

`counterbalance.optimise` searches instead for an assignment whose lists have
near-equal totals on the dimensions you name, by exchanging pairs of item sets
between lists. List sizes are preserved, since a swap trades one set for another.

```yaml
counterbalance:
  lists: 4
  optimise: true
  balance_on: [length, n_density, old20, frequency]
```

`balance_on` defaults to `match_on`, and the example adds frequency. Frequency is
the manipulated variable and so is not matched on, but it is manipulated *within*
a list, since every list holds both conditions. Equating the lists on its total
therefore costs the manipulation nothing and removes a difference between the
participant groups who receive different lists. Naming only the matched dimensions
leaves frequency dealt arbitrarily. In `design_en_balanced_lists.yaml`, the
optimiser then improves the three named dimensions and makes frequency worse than
the arbitrary deal had it. Balance what you want equated across lists, which is
usually everything.

The optimiser's search is a steepest descent to a local optimum, not a global
search. It guarantees that no single exchange would improve matters further, unless
`counterbalance.max_passes`, 500 passes by default, stops the search first. In that
case, the datasheet and the run log say so, and a higher bound may balance the
lists further. The datasheet records the imbalance before and after, so the
improvement is checkable. The objective is all-integer and ties are broken by the
seeded keyed hash, which keeps the two engines on the same assignment and stops
list 1 being favoured for being numbered first.

Optimisation is off by default, and the default will not change. Switching it on
changes which items a participant sees, so the researcher has to choose it in the
design. A package upgrade must never make that change for a study that is already
running. It is rejected on a Latin-square design, where every item already appears
in every list and the lists are balanced on the items by construction.
`balance_lists()` runs the search alone if you want the assignment without applying
it, and `design_en_balanced_lists.yaml` is the worked example.

Each dimension is counted in a unit of its own before the totals are compared. By
default, the unit is the dimension's mean, which suits ratio scales only. A
dimension then weighs in proportion to its SD over its mean, so its weight depends
on where its scale starts. Zipf frequency starts near 3, and in
`design_en_balanced_lists.yaml` it counts for least of the four dimensions.
Rewriting it as Zipf - 3 would move 22 of the 40 item sets to another list.
`counterbalance.scale: mad` counts each dimension's deviations from its mean in
units of its mean absolute deviation. The values are rounded to hundredths first,
so adding a constant that is a whole number of hundredths leaves the lists as they
were. The default stays `mean` so that a study already running keeps its lists,
and under `mad` the datasheet and the Methods text name the scale.

## Practice, fillers and feedback

A single data frame can serve as the materials record and as the experiment's trial
list only while the two contain the same trials, and they usually do not. Practice
exists to settle the participant into the task and is discarded before analysis.
Fillers exist to dilute the manipulation so the participant cannot guess it, and
are likewise not analysed. Both have to reach the generated experiment, and neither
belongs in the stimuli file, the descriptives or the realised control.

The pipeline therefore writes the stimuli CSV and the reports from the main rows
and generates the PsychoPy, OpenSesame and jsPsych experiments from every presented
trial. A `block` column marks which is which, and it appears only when a design
declares the blocks.

```yaml
practice:
  path: items/practice_en_lexdec.csv
fillers:
  path: items/fillers_en_lexdec.csv
```

Where each block goes is a methodological choice. Practice comes first, as its
own run, ordered within itself by the seeded keyed hash, so every participant
given a list and trial order sees the practice items in one fixed order. Fillers
are interleaved with the main trials, because a block of fillers at the end would
be a second block the participant can tell apart. They are merged in before the
order is drawn, so one deterministic shuffle mixes them through. This renumbers the
main trials, since adding fillers changes the sequence, and the stimuli file
records where each item appeared.

Both blocks appear in every list and neither is counterbalanced, because they
carry no manipulation to rotate and every participant should get the same
practice. In a resampled design, the copy of a list in each replicate is a
presentation version of its own, and it gets both blocks too. The PsychoPy,
OpenSesame and jsPsych experiments pause where the practice trials end and nowhere
else, since a pause around a filler would set it apart.

Each block's item table is read with the same validation as any other and given a
`set` range that cannot collide with the main items. Without that range, practice
item 1 and main item 1 would both be set 1. The counts and the tables' checksums go
into the datasheet, because what the participant saw is part of the materials even
when it is not part of the analysis.

A `feedback` event scores the trial and shows the result. It reads the field named
by `answer`, compares it as a string with the key the participant pressed, and
displays `correct`, `incorrect` or `no_response` for `duration_ms`.

```yaml
- type: feedback
  answer: answer
  correct: 'Correct'
  incorrect: 'Incorrect'
  no_response: 'Too slow'
  duration_ms: 600
  blocks: [practice]
```

`blocks:` restricts an event to the named blocks. Its main use is to limit feedback
to practice, where it confirms the mapping the instructions state. In the task
itself, feedback would contaminate reaction times. The restriction has to be
expressed on the event because the event list is global to the design. A feedback
event scores a keypress, so a design whose feedback event has no preceding
`response` or `question` is rejected when the experiment is generated. Left to run
time, the error would appear as a different failure in each of the three targets.
`design_en_lexdec_blocks.yaml` combines practice, fillers and feedback.

## The three presentation targets

All three exporters take the same rendered event list, so the procedure is the
same in each. What differs is what each platform can do.

```{r export}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "lexsync_experiment")
dir.create(out, showWarnings = FALSE)
files <- export_experiments(stim, design, schema, out)
basename(unlist(files[c("psychopy", "opensesame", "jspsych")]))
```

`export_experiments()` calls `assign_triggers()` first, then each exporter, and
returns the three experiment scripts, with every file it wrote listed as `files`.
The directory holds more than the scripts.

```{r export-dir}
list.files(out)
```

PsychoPy and OpenSesame read their trials at run time from CSV tables written
beside the scripts. PsychoPy has one table and OpenSesame two, since OpenSesame's
text is kept apart from its loop table, for the reason given below. The jsPsych
target embeds its trials in the HTML, and that single file is enough to reproduce
the procedure in a browser.

Two schema settings shape the display. `presentation$text_height_px`, a whole
number from 8 to 400 and 48 by default, is the height of the stimulus text in
pixels in all three targets. In OpenSesame, the setting is the experiment's
`font_size`, which every screen uses, the instructions included.
`presentation$fullscreen`, true by default, runs the PsychoPy script full screen, as
PsychoPy's advice on reducing dropped frames recommends. With false, the script
opens a 1280 x 1024 window. OpenSesame takes full screen or a window from the mode
it is launched in, and the generated file's `fullscreen` line has no effect.

PsychoPy (Peirce et al., 2019) is the reference target. The generated script
carries the event list as embedded JSON and interprets it, and it writes onset
triggers to the parallel port, or to a serial device, locked to the flip. It is the
target to use for EEG.

The script reads keys from PsychoPy's `keyboard` module. A response window opens on
a flip, where the keyboard's clock is reset and its queue cleared, so a reaction
time runs from that flip and a key pressed before it does not count. Before the
first trial, the script shows the version's instructions and waits for the space
bar. Escape there ends the run before a data file is opened.

Each run writes a data file under `data/` beside the script, named
`<base>_p<participant>_v<version>_<date>-<time>.csv`, without the `_p` part when no
participant number is given. It holds one row per trial, written as the trial ends,
so a run stopped with escape leaves a valid file of the trials it completed.

A row gives the participant, the version, the replicate and the list, then the
trial's own fields and trigger codes, then what the trial recorded. `response`,
`rt_ms` and `timed_out` hold the key, its reaction time in milliseconds and whether
the window closed without one. The reaction time runs from the onset of the
stimulus the key answers, or from the opening of a window kept with `from: offset`.
`correct` says whether the key was the trial's `answer`. It is 0 after a timeout
and empty when the trial names no answer. In a design without a response event, the
question's key is the one scored. `region_rts_ms` holds each self-paced reading
region's time, joined by `|`, and `question_response` and `question_rt_ms` the
question's key and reaction time. Near its end, the row gives the measured
`refresh_hz` and `trigger_mode`, which is `hardware` when the codes went to the
device and `mock` when they were printed. It ends with `event_flips` and
`event_onsets_ms`: the flips each event took and the time of its first flip
relative to the trial's first flip, joined by `|` in event order. A stimulus that
collects its response counts the blank after it as well, up to the key or the close
of the window. The realised durations can be checked against the declared ones
there.

OpenSesame (Mathôt et al., 2012) is generated as a plain-text `.osexp`, block by
block, with each event becoming an inline script. Each script builds its canvases
before the trial runs, in its prepare phase, and its event is timed from the onset
its display returns. The experiment sends its triggers by a different method from
PsychoPy's. Its setup opens the device `triggers$backend` names, the parallel port
or the serial port `triggers$serial_port`, and follows `triggers$mode` when it
cannot open it. The method and these settings are described under 'Trigger timing
and the flip lock' below. By default, the setup prints the codes and carries on, so
the experiment still runs on a machine without the hardware, and an inline script
after the setup, `lexsync_trigger_notice`, says so before any other screen.

OpenSesame also evaluates what its loop table holds. In both versions, a cell
holding `[=...]` runs as Python, and so does one holding a single `{` in
OpenSesame 4.x, where it is read as an f-string, or starting with `=` in 3.3.
Both versions retype a word such as `nan` or `007`, and 4.x shows `True` as 1. In
4.x, `infinity` and `nan`, both in the English lexicon, stop the session. Unchecked,
an item table passed between laboratories could run code on the machine that
presents it.

The loop table, `vignette_experiment_english_opensesame.csv` here, therefore
holds numbers only: `lexsync_row`, the trial's position in loop order, with
`lexsync_trial`, `lexsync_list`, `lexsync_set`, the trigger codes,
`critical_region` and any per-trial duration. The prefix matters because
OpenSesame 4 makes every loop column a global of the inline scripts, where `list`
and `set` would shadow Python's built-in functions of those names. The presented
text, `condition`, `block` and `answer` are in
`vignette_experiment_english_opensesame_text.csv`, which the setup script reads
with Python's `csv` module, and each script looks up its trial's row by
`lexsync_row`. Copy both files with the experiment. A value in a numeric column
that is not a plain number is rejected when the experiment is generated. The
feedback script reads the response without evaluation, so a timeout shows its
`no_response` text in both versions. These rules were checked against the
sources of OpenSesame 3.3.14 and 4.1.20.

```{r opensesame-tables}
opensesame_csv <- file.path(out, "vignette_experiment_english_opensesame.csv")
names(read.csv(opensesame_csv))
names(read.csv(sub("\\.csv$", "_text.csv", opensesame_csv)))
```

OpenSesame writes nothing to its log file without a logger item, so every trial
ends with one, `lexsync_logger`, which writes every variable. The word and its
response window are one inline script. It shows the word, sends the trigger, then
flushes the keyboard and polls it while the word is shown and over a blank screen
after it. It sets `response`, `response_time` (from the word's onset), `timed_out`
and `correct`, the last scored against the trial's `answer` by the script itself.
OpenSesame's own `correct_response` is not used, since its variable syntax differs
between 3.3 and 4.x.

A response kept after the stimulus with `from: offset` is a `keyboard_response`
after a blank screen, followed by a script that sets `timed_out` and `correct`. A
`keyboard_response` runs none of lexsync's code, so the script that shows the blank
first waits until the hold of any code still on the port is up. After a stimulus
shorter than the hold, the window therefore opens when the hold is up, and
`response_time`, which OpenSesame times from the item's start, runs from there.

Self-paced reading sets `lexsync_region_rts`, and a question sets
`question_response` and `question_rt`. Each trial clears these before its first
event. Before the logger, a script copies the trial's `condition`, `block` and
`answer` from the text table into `lexsync_condition`, `lexsync_block` and
`lexsync_answer`. Both versions' loggers write a variable without evaluating it.

Before the loop, an inline script, `lexsync_instructions`, shows the instructions
and waits for the space bar, and escape there stops the session. OpenSesame's
canvas reads a subset of HTML, so the script writes the text with `&`, `<` and `>`
escaped and each line break as `<br />`. In a design with practice trials, an
inline script, `lexsync_block_break`, opens every trial. On the first trial after
the practice trials, it says that they have ended and waits for the space bar, as
the PsychoPy and jsPsych experiments do. It reads each trial's block from the text
table, so the experiment needs no run-if condition, a syntax that differs between
OpenSesame 3.3 and 4.x.

jsPsych is the browser target, suitable for behavioural work, piloting and sharing
a procedure, though never for EEG. A browser cannot address a parallel port, so the
trigger codes go into each trial's data and no marker leaves the machine. The
generated HTML embeds the events and the trials, opens with a welcome screen that
shows the instructions and waits for the space bar, and saves responses locally, so
no server is needed. The word and its response window are one jsPsych trial,
recorded with `lexsync_event` set to `target`. It accepts the response keys from
the word's onset, shows the word for its duration and runs on for the timeout. The
first key ends it, and its `rt` is timed from the word's onset.

The jsPsych library, its keyboard-response plugin and its stylesheet load from a
CDN, so the first run needs an internet connection. Each of the three files is
loaded with Subresource Integrity, its SHA-384 and `crossorigin="anonymous"`, so
the browser will not load a copy that differs from the published release. A page
that collects participants' responses therefore runs only the code it was written
with. To run offline, point the tags at downloaded copies and serve the folder over
http, or remove each tag's `integrity` and `crossorigin` attributes. A browser
blocks the CORS request that a page opened from a `file://` address would make for
a local copy, so it could not check the hash.

Two details of the generated files keep the three targets consistent. The
OpenSesame loop is written as `sequential`, because its default is random, which
would discard the seeded trial order and make the three targets present different
sequences. That order is computed from the design by a keyed-hash shuffle and is
identical in the R and Python engines. The jsPsych exporter maps the event model's
key names onto browser key names, so `left` becomes `arrowleft`.

```{r loop-table}
psychopy_csv <- file.path(out, "vignette_experiment_english_psychopy.csv")
names(read.csv(psychopy_csv))
```

The trial table carries exactly the columns the events reference plus the
bookkeeping ones. A field no event mentions is not exported.

## Running a counterbalanced experiment

A design with more than one list, or with resampled item sets, has several
presentation versions. A version is one (replicate, list) pair of the presented
trials, and the versions are numbered from 1 in that order, so in a design without
replicates version *k* is list *k*. Each participant is presented one version.
Presenting them all would show every item sample of a resampled design, and would
show each target of a Latin square in every condition, which is the repetition the
rotation exists to prevent. Participant *p* runs version `((p - 1) mod V) + 1` of
the *V* versions, the rule `participant_table()` allocates by.

```{r versions}
two <- utils::modifyList(design, list(name = "vignette_two_lists",
                                      counterbalance = list(lists = 2)))
two_files <- export_experiments(counterbalance(stim, two, schema), two, schema, out)
basename(grep("\\.osexp$", two_files$files, value = TRUE))
participant_table(list(list = 1:2), 4)
```

The PsychoPy script runs the participant's version when launched as
`python <base>_psychopy.py --participant 3`. `--version 2` runs a version outright,
and so does `--list 2` in a design without replicates. Launched with none of these,
the script asks for the participant number and the version in a dialogue. Leaving
the version blank selects the participant's version by the rule above. A version
the script does not have stops the run, with a message, before any window opens.

The jsPsych page reads the same choice from its address: `page.html?participant=3`,
`?version=2` or, in a design without replicates, `?list=2`, each a whole number
from 1. A page with more than one version, opened with none of these, shows a
screen saying how to open it and runs nothing. A static page cannot count its
participants, so a study recruited online without participant numbers hands out one
`?version=k` link per version. The welcome screen counts the trials of the version,
every data row carries the participant, the version, the list and the replicate,
and the data file is named `<title>_p<participant>_v<version>.csv`.

The OpenSesame target writes one experiment per version, as above:
`<base>_list<k>.osexp`, or `<base>_rep<r>_list<k>.osexp` when the versions span
several replicates. A design with one version and one trial order keeps
`<base>.osexp`. Each experiment has its own loop and text tables, holding only that
version's trials, and the experimenter opens the participant's. At start-up, each
experiment compares the subject number OpenSesame asks for with its own version.
When that participant would normally run another one, it says so and waits for a
key. Space goes on with this file, and escape stops the session. The check runs
once, before the loop, so the experiment needs no run-if condition.

The datasheet records the number of versions as `counterbalancing$versions` and
the rule as `counterbalancing$assignment`, and its Methods text says that each
participant was presented one version. Its artefact list and the run log name every
file `export_experiments()` wrote, the loop and text tables included, since those
hold the trial order and the trigger codes the experiments present. The loop tables
keep each version's trials together, ordered by replicate, list and trial. They
carry `replicate` when the design has one. Item codes are allocated by set, so in a
resampled design an item code identifies an item only within its replicate, which
the `replicate` column tells apart.

With `counterbalance.orders: m` (see 'Trial orders and runs of one condition'
above), each version also has m trial orders. Participant *p* runs order
`(((p - 1) div V) mod m) + 1`. In a two-list design with two orders, participants 1
and 2 run lists 1 and 2 in order 1, participants 3 and 4 run them in order 2, and
participant 5 starts the cycle again. The PsychoPy script and the jsPsych page sort
the version's trials by the participant's order, and a run without a participant
number presents order 1. Their data rows then carry the order, and their `trial`
column numbers the trials as presented. The OpenSesame target writes one experiment
per version and order, `<base>_list<k>_order<j>.osexp`, or
`<base>_rep<r>_list<k>_order<j>.osexp` when the versions span several replicates
and `<base>_order<j>.osexp` for a design with one version. Each experiment's check
compares the order as well as the version, and every trial logs `lexsync_order`.

## Trigger timing and the flip lock

The timing of the trigger is what justifies generating the experiment. An ERP is
averaged over epochs cut around a marker, so the marker's timing error propagates
straight into the waveform. If the trigger is sent when the code decides to draw
the stimulus rather than when the display shows it, the error is the interval
between those two moments. That interval is up to one refresh, about 17 ms at
60 Hz, plus whatever the drawing code took, and it varies from trial to trial. A
constant offset can be subtracted afterwards, but jitter cannot, and it smears the
average and shrinks the component you are measuring.

The generated PsychoPy script never sends a trigger from the drawing sequence.
It registers the write with the window, to be executed on the next flip:

```
win.callOnFlip(port.setData, trigger)
```

`callOnFlip` defers the call until the flip that puts the stimulus on screen, so
the port write happens in the same operation that makes the stimulus visible.
The Python package's test suite checks this property of the generated code by
driving the generated script against a mock PsychoPy window and a mock port and
asserting that the trigger is bound to the flip.

The reset is handled the same way. A recorder needs the line to return to zero
before the next code, so the script counts the hold down flip by flip and queues a
write of 0 on the flip that ends it. A code whose stimulus is shorter than the hold,
such as a one-flip prime, stays on the port through the events that follow and is
reset on that flip all the same. Only the next onset's code ends it sooner, with a 0
written just before the new code. The session markers, 254 before the first trial
and 255 after the last, are held the same way.

```{r trigger-settings}
str(schema$triggers)
```

`trigger_hold_ms` is 50, comfortably above the 10 ms minimum most recorders need
to register a pulse. The script converts it to the nearest whole number of flips at
the refresh it measures, and never to fewer than the flips that cover 10 ms. The
pulse therefore stays about 50 ms whether the display runs at 60 Hz or at 240 Hz,
where a hold of three frames, 50 ms at 60 Hz, would last 12.5 ms.
`reset_after_frames: N`, read only when `trigger_hold_ms` is not set, gives a hold
of N + 1 frames at `presentation.assumed_refresh_hz`. `inter_trigger_ms` is accepted
but not used, since the self-paced reading critical-region code is held like every
other code, and the run log says so when a schema sets it. `parallel_address` is
the LPT1 base address on a typical laboratory machine, and it is a schema value
because it belongs to the machine, which will run many designs.
`allow_code_overlap` is false, so a design whose item codes cannot all be kept
apart from its other codes is rejected, as described under 'Triggers on an event'
above.

`backend` names the device both laboratory targets write the codes to. `parallel`,
the default, is the port at `parallel_address`. `serial` writes each code as one
byte to the device that `serial_port` names, at `baudrate` bits per second, 115200
unless set. A schema for a serial device therefore adds `backend: serial`, the port
as `serial_port: COM3` (`/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux) and the rate the device's manual
gives. The port has to be named, and a serial backend without one is rejected. A
code is held and reset on a serial device as on a parallel port, with a 0 written
when its hold is up.

A serial line delays each code by an amount that varies from code to code, and a
parallel port does not. A USB-serial adapter carries each byte in a USB transfer,
scheduled in frames of a millisecond on a full-speed connection, and its driver
adds a delay of its own. Adapters built on FTDI chips also hold data on its way to
the computer until their latency timer runs out, 16 ms by default. That matters for
a device that answers and for a response box on the same adapter. Measure the delay
with a photodiode, as described under 'Checking the timing' below.

`mode` decides what happens when the device cannot be opened, as on a laptop with
no parallel port. Under `auto`, the default, both targets print each code in the
console, and a screen before any other tells the experimenter that no codes will be
sent. Pressing C goes on without them, and escape stops the run. Under `hardware`,
when the device cannot be opened, the PsychoPy script stops before its window opens
and the OpenSesame experiment stops in its setup. `mock` prints the codes without
trying the device, after the same notice. Every trial records the mode the run
used, `hardware` or `mock`, as `trigger_mode` in the PsychoPy data file and as
`lexsync_trigger_mode` in the OpenSesame log.

OpenSesame has no `callOnFlip`, so the generated inline script sends the trigger
on the line after the canvas is shown:

```
_t0 = _lexsync_c_e1.show()
var.onset_time = _t0
_lexsync_onset(int(var.get(u'condition_trigger', _eval=False)), _t0)
```

`show()` blocks until the display refresh and returns at it, so the next statement
runs immediately after the stimulus becomes visible. The canvas was built in the
script's prepare phase, before the trial started, so nothing delays the show. The
residual offset is the few microseconds of the return and the port write, and it
is constant rather than jittered. The method therefore comes close to the flip lock
without matching it, which is why PsychoPy stays the reference target for EEG.

`_lexsync_onset` notes when the code is due to be reset, and the waits after it
reset the code once `trigger_hold_ms` has passed, in a later event when this one is
shorter. The setup script measures the frame period at start-up and logs it as
`lexsync_frame_ms`, and each event ends half a frame before its duration is up.
OpenSesame's legacy clock counts whole milliseconds, so the waits are kept to the
millisecond, and so is a hold that ends during one. A hold that ends while the
experiment waits for the next refresh lasts until that display, up to a frame
longer. One that ends after the last wait of a trial lasts until the next trial's
first display. Between trials, the logger and the next trial's prepare phase run
while the last display stays up, so a trial's last event lasts a little longer than
its duration.

Neither generation nor its tests import PsychoPy, pyserial or any port driver,
since generation only writes text. The hardware is needed only to run an
experiment, so the demonstration reproduces on a laptop.

### Checking the timing

The durations above are what the generated code asks for, and what the Python
package's tests confirm on simulated displays. A real display adds delays no
software can detect, such as an LCD's input lag. A study whose effect depends on a
duration or an onset should therefore be measured on the machine that will run it.
A photodiode on the screen, recorded by the same amplifier as the trigger port,
measures the display and the triggers on one clock.

1. Tape the photodiode over the place where the critical stimulus appears. White
   text on a black background drives most diodes. A small stimulus, such as a
   fixation cross, may need a white patch drawn with it for the pilot.
2. Run a pilot session on the laboratory machine, at the refresh rate and in the
   screen mode of the study, and record the diode and the trigger channel together.
   With `triggers.mode: hardware`, neither the pilot nor the study can start without
   the trigger device.
3. For each trial, measure the time from the trigger's onset to the diode's rise.
   It should be nearly constant. Its mean is the display's lag, which includes the
   time the screen takes to draw down to the diode and, on an LCD, an input lag
   that can exceed 10 ms. The analysis can subtract it. Its spread is the jitter an
   ERP average will carry.
4. Measure each critical stimulus from the diode's rise to its fall and compare it
   with the flips its duration asks for at that refresh rate: a 50 ms prime is
   three flips at 60 Hz and seven, 48.6 ms, at 144 Hz.
5. Measure the trigger pulses. Each should last about `trigger_hold_ms`, 50 ms by
   default, unless the next onset ends it sooner, and 254 should come before the
   first trial and 255 after the last.
6. Measure again after any change to the machine, the display, its refresh rate or
   the presentation software.

## Adding a paradigm

A design can override the event list outright, which needs no change to the
package. The events below present a word twice with a mask between, which no
registered paradigm does, and both `text` events are triggered so the recording
can distinguish the two presentations.

```{r custom-events}
custom <- design
custom$name <- "vignette_custom"
custom$events <- list(
  list(type = "fixation", content = "+", duration_frames = 30L),
  list(type = "text", content = "{word}", duration_frames = 12L,
       trigger = 30L, onset_locked = TRUE),
  list(type = "mask", content = "#####", duration_frames = 6L),
  list(type = "text", content = "{word}", duration_frames = 48L,
       trigger = "condition", onset_locked = TRUE),
  list(type = "response", keys = c("left", "right"), timeout_ms = 2000L),
  list(type = "blank", duration_frames = 15L)
)
required_fields(custom)
custom_files <- export_experiments(stim, custom, schema, out)
basename(unlist(custom_files[c("psychopy", "opensesame", "jspsych")]))
```

All three targets rendered the new sequence without a change to the backends,
because each interprets the event list and no backend holds a paradigm's event
sequence. Declaring events changes only the trial. The counterbalancing recipe
still follows the paradigm the design names, `factorial` here, and a design that
names no paradigm counterbalances factorially.

To register a paradigm for reuse across designs, add an entry to the `PARADIGMS`
registry in `R/paradigms.R`, giving its `stimulus_fields`, its `counterbalance`
recipe and its `events`, and add the matching entry to
`python_workflow/src/lexsync/paradigms.py` so that the two engines keep the same
registry. Designs can then name it. The registry is a plain named list and the
entries above are the pattern to copy.

To add a presentation target, write an `export_<target>()` that interprets the
same rendered event list, and it will serve every paradigm.
